body: NVDA shares reverse Wednesday's gains following a report that Nvidia's CEO had a relationship with an executive reporting to him. If confirmed, the allegations could add a new corporate-governance problem to the company's existing leadership controversy. Nvidia (NVDA) shares are falling sharply in after-hours trading following a new report from The New York Times alleging that CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a company executive who reports to him. According to a market quote captured at 00:11 GMT+2 on November 12, NVDA traded at $167.37 after hours, down $6.36 or 3.66% from Wednesday's regular-session close of $173.73. The decline reverses more than Wednesday's 2.87% regular-session gain. The New York Times reported the new allegation late Wednesday, adding another potential complication for Nvidia's board of directors. The company is already investigating Huang following earlier reports concerning his relationship with a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence reportedly identified as having connections to Chinese intelligence. That earlier controversy raised questions about national security, corporate oversight and whether sensitive information could have been compromised. The latest allegation, however, introduces a potentially different concern. If Huang had a relationship with an executive who reported directly to him, investors could reasonably question whether there were conflicts of interest involving management decisions, compensation, promotions or internal corporate governance. A personal relationship does not, by itself, establish wrongdoing or improper conduct. The significance depends on the circumstances, the company's policies, what was disclosed to the board and whether any business decisions were affected. The new allegation has not been independently verified by investingLive. Jensen Huang is not an ordinary corporate CEO. He co-founded Nvidia and has been central to its transformation into one of the world's most important artificial intelligence companies. For shareholders, the concern is not simply the executive's personal conduct. It is whether repeated controversies could undermine confidence in Nvidia's leadership, distract management or increase pressure on its board. Corporate governance: Investors may demand clearer answers about how Nvidia's board oversees its CEO and manages potential conflicts of interest. Leadership continuity: Any widening of the investigation could raise further questions about succession planning at a company closely associated with its founder. Valuation and investor confidence: Even without changes to Nvidia's chip demand, earnings or competitive position, greater uncertainty about leadership could influence how much investors are willing to pay for the stock. That does not mean Huang will leave Nvidia or that the allegations will ultimately affect the company's operations. But investors may increasingly distinguish between confidence in Nvidia's AI business and confidence in its corporate leadership. The immediate question is whether the after-hours selling continues when regular U.S. trading resumes Thursday, November 12. The reported decline comes while the Nasdaq futures market is closed, limiting the ability to draw conclusions about the broader technology sector's reaction at that moment. Traders should monitor whether Nvidia underperforms the Nasdaq and semiconductor stocks once futures trading resumes, and whether the company or its board responds to the latest reporting. A recovery toward Wednesday's $173.73 closing price would suggest the initial selling is being absorbed. Sustained weakness would raise the possibility that investors are assigning a greater risk premium to Nvidia's leadership uncertainty. For now, the market is reacting to another allegation rather than a confirmed finding of misconduct. title: Who Will Buy Sable’s Oil if California Keeps Closing Refineries?
summary: Situated off California’s Santa Barbara coast, the Santa Ynez project operated by Sable Offshore has become a litmus test of President Trump’s determination to revive oil production in a state pursuing a future beyond it. body: Natalia Katona is a freelance commodity analyst, based in the United Arab Emirates. Situated off California’s Santa Barbara coast, the Santa Ynez project operated by Sable Offshore has become a litmus test of President Trump’s determination to revive oil production in a state pursuing a future beyond it. After a decade of shutdowns, its return depended on the Trump administration’s intervention in a prolonged regulatory battle. Originally developed by ExxonMobil, the Santa Ynez complex comprises the Hondo, Harmony and Heritage platforms and their associated onshore infrastructure. Its troubles began in May 2015, when Plains All American’s Line 901 pipeline ruptured due to external corrosion near Refugio State Beach, spilling almost 3,000 barrels of crude . The failure cut off the project’s route to local refineries and broader market, forcing production to stop. ExxonMobil eventually sold the assets to Sable in 2024 for a total consideration of $643 million . Restarting the production proved difficult. Pipeline safety requirements, permitting disputes and court orders kept the development from returning to normal operations. Those obstacles unfolded against Democrat-led California’s broader push to reduce its dependence on fossil fuels: in 2021, Governor Gavin Newsom asked state regulators to analyze how to phase out oil extraction by 2045 . Sable announced in May 2025 that it had restarted production from Harmony, a claim California officials disputed , saying the activity was well testing. The offshore platforms sit in federal waters, beyond the state’s direct reach, but the oil initially went into storage while its onshore pipeline route, which California regulated at the time, remained blocked. The Trump administration then helped reopen that route in two steps. In December 2025, the federal Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) reclassified the onshore pipelines as interstate infrastructure at Sable’s request, asserting federal oversight, and approved their restart plan on Dec. 22 . After the conflict between the US and Iran started in late February 2026, just as the ensuing energy crisis hit the markets, Energy Secretary Chris Wright invoked the Defense Production Act to direct the restoration of operations on March 13 , citing supply risks and military dependence on foreign oil. Sable resumed pipeline shipments the following day. However, California’s Democratic administration challenged both interventions, turning the project’s revival into a continuing fight over federal and state authority. Democratic control of the House and Senate, won in the early November midterms , will not automatically reverse those decisions. The new Congress takes office in January, while Trump retains executive authority and the ability to veto legislation. But congressional committees can investigate the administration’s intervention, demand records and use spending negotiations to seek restrictions. Members of California’s congressional delegation have already started: in May they wrote to Sable’s CEO asking the company to preserve records and promising continued oversight in the next Congress. For Sable, the likely exposure is greater scrutiny and less scope for additional legislative support, rather than an immediate congressional shutdown. Courts remain the more direct threat to the legal foundations of its pipeline operations. Sable CEO Jim Flores said on the company’s earnings call that the rulings it has won, including one upholding PHMSA’s jurisdiction over the pipeline, are on appeal at the Ninth Circuit. That uncertainty matters because the commercial margin for disruption is already narrow. title: Hot U.S. CPI and High Real Yields Keep Gold Under Pressure - FXEmpire
body: It starts the day with a couple of influences pulling in opposite directions. We have elevated U.S. real yields raising the financing costs of holding non-interest-bearing assets, while the metal continues to retain a high nominal price following a year of geopolitical and inflation chaos. The latest official available settlement date listed the December 2026 COMEX gold contract at $4,074.90. The real-rate backdrop remains restrictive. The U.S. Treasuryâs daily real yield curve placed the 5-year real yield at 2.35% and the 10-year yield at 2.63% on November 6. Across every business day that week, the 5-year measure remained between 2.31% and 2.39%, with the 10-year yield staying between 2.60% and 2.65%. These are derived TIPS par yields. They donât establish a mechanical inverse relationship with gold, but they do represent part of the opportunity cost and a high hurdle for an asset that produces no coupon or interest payments. On Tuesday, the BLS reported Core CPI at 0.3% , above the expected 0.2%, and CPI m/m at 0.4%, higher than the expected 0.3% for the month of October. This continues to be a thorn in the side of doves, and should continue to put pressure on the Fed to remain restrictive. Fridayâs labor report gave the market an additional policy input that shouldnât be ignored. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that nonfarm payroll employment increased by 165,000 jobs in October, while the unemployment rate came in at 4.1%. The labor market is still expanding, which can reduce pressure for rapid monetary easing, although payrolls alone donât determine Federal Reserve policy. Nonetheless, more employment typically means that more consumers are out there, with inflation having that input. For gold, the overall relevant information runs through expected policy rates, nominal Treasury yields, inflation compensation, and the dollar, rather than just through employment itself. A higher inflation reading supports goldâs store-of-wealth narrative, but it could also lift yields if investors expect a firmer policy path. A softer reading could reduce nominal and real yields while also weakening demand for inflation protection. The shape of the real yield curve also deserves attention. On November 6, the 30-year real yield was 3.07%, above the 20-year rate of 2.91% and the 10-year rate of 2.63%. This upward slope implies investors demand progressively more inflation-adjusted return at longer maturities. For the gold market, the long end can matter through portfolio allocation and the cost of carrying defensive positions. A fall confined to short maturities would be less supportive than a broad decline across the entire curve. Every new Gold analysis as it publishes, today's technical signal and key levels, live price â on one page. BLS reported on November 5 that third-quarter nonfarm business productivity rose at a 3.6% seasonally adjusted annual rate, with output up 3.7% and hours worked up 0.1%. Unit labor costs fell 0.7% during the quarter but were 2.4% higher than a year earlier. Strong productivity can allow output and wages to grow with less inflationary pressure, potentially modifying and moderating the monetary premium embedded in gold. The near-term narrative depends on whether real yields break out of last weekâs narrow, elevated range and what the reaction to subsequent inputs is this week. For what it is worth, the gold market gapped higher to kick off the trading session and has since fallen. It still looks very much like a market that is struggling to get above $4,200, and with the 50-day EMA sitting just above, the technical outlook for this market suggests stagnation, possibly even weakness. A daily close above $4,250 would change my attitude on this, though.

title: Gold Price Recovers Above US$4,000 As Analysts Forecast Further Gains - DirectorsTalk Interviews
body: Gold prices recovered on 11 November after falling sharply in the previous session, with the precious metal holding above the US$4,000 per ounce level despite renewed concerns over inflation and the prospect of higher US interest rates. Spot gold traded around US$4,040 per ounce, following a decline of approximately 3% on Tuesday. Stronger-than-expected US inflation data and expectations of further Federal Reserve tightening had contributed to the earlier selling pressure. The latest recovery comes as analysts assess whether the recent correction represents a temporary setback or a change in the broader direction of the gold market. The US$4,000 level has emerged as an important support area, with prices managing to remain above it despite pressure from higher bond yields and a stronger US dollar. Standard Chartered maintains a positive outlook, forecasting an average gold price of US$4,650 per ounce during the fourth quarter of 2026, followed by a further increase to US$4,850 in the first quarter of 2027. The bank points to continued investment demand and central bank purchases as important sources of support. Gold-backed exchange-traded products attracted 211 tonnes of investment demand during the third quarter, their strongest quarterly inflows since 2024. A further 19 tonnes entered these products during October. Central bank purchases also remained significant, reaching 321 tonnes in the third quarter, above Standard Chartered’s estimate of 200 tonnes. Continued official-sector buying has provided an additional source of demand as central banks diversify their reserves. The bank also considers gold’s ability to maintain support above US$4,000 despite stronger economic data an indication of underlying market resilience. However, a move above US$4,200 would represent the next significant technical level to watch. CPM Group has also maintained a constructive view of the precious metals market following the recent correction. The research group considers the latest decline a period of consolidation following several days of gains, rather than evidence that the broader upward trend has ended. Its assessment points to continued demand for precious metals amid concerns surrounding economic uncertainty, government debt, inflation and geopolitical developments. Uncertainty over technology company valuations and wider financial market conditions has also contributed to interest in alternative stores of value. body: Nvidia 's stock (NASDAQ: NVDA) closed at a record high of $239.24 per share on Oct. 6. But today, the AI chipmaker 's stock trades at about $175. Let's see what caused that 27% decline -- and where Nvidia's stock might be trading by the end of next year. Nvidia is the world's largest producer of discrete GPUs. It originally sold most of those chips to PC gamers, but it now generates most of its revenue from the data center market. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » Unlike CPUs, which are optimized for fast sequential processing, GPUs are designed to execute thousands of calculations simultaneously through massive parallelism. That key difference makes GPUs better suited for training AI models than stand-alone CPUs. Nvidia's early mover's advantage enabled it to dominate the AI data center market with its chips, and it locks in those customers with its proprietary software and services. Today, most of the world's top AI companies -- including Anthropic and OpenAI -- use Nvidia's GPUs. From fiscal 2021 to fiscal 2026 (which ended this January), Nvidia's revenue grew from $16.7 billion to $215.9 billion, while its net income jumped from $4.3 billion to $120.1 billion. Even after its latest decline, its stock is still up roughly 1,210% over the past six years. Nvidia's market dominance and breakneck growth made it one of the easiest ways to profit from the AI boom. But with 93% of its revenue coming from the data center market in its latest quarter, it could only maintain its momentum if AI companies kept buying more chips. Over the past year, the Iran war, inflation, and the Fed's interest rate hike in September drove more investors to question that bullish thesis. As the costs of building new data centers outpaced the monetization of new AI services, it became harder to justify those expenses. The Democratic sweep of the midterm elections on Nov. 3 exacerbated that pressure. Several newly elected officials -- including Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa -- have called for moratoriums on new data centers until tighter regulations are rolled out. On Nov. 8, Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang admitted that he had an extramarital affair in a public company memo. Huang didn't name anyone, but the major media outlets pointed at Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed. This Singapore-based cloud computing firm that spent at least $4.8 billion on Nvidia's data center chips over the past three years. On its own, this partnership didn't violate any laws. However, Megaspeed allegedly sold those AI chips to Chinese tech companies and violated the export curbs against China. Several reports also called Alice Huang a Chinese spy, an allegation that China denies. Those accusations are troubling because another one of Nvidia's major customers, California-based Supermicro (NASDAQ: SMCI), was recently hit with similar allegations. Supermicro's co-founder, Yih-Shyan Liaw, and two others were recently indicted for conspiring to smuggle $2.5 billion in Nvidia-equipped servers to China through Asian shell companies. It's unclear whether Nvidia turned a blind eye to these activities or simply failed to track them, but the allegations have prompted the company's board to open an internal investigation. It also faces new government probes and a massive class action lawsuit from its shareholders. Nvidia is still growing rapidly, and the market's demand for its chips is still outstripping its supply. From fiscal 2026 to fiscal 2029, analysts expect its revenue and EPS to both grow at a 61% CAGR. That's an incredible growth rate for a stock trading at 17 times this year's earnings. title: AMD Stock Jumps 9.5% to $564 as CoreWeave Results and UBS CPU Report Reignite Wall Street's AI Chip Trade - International Business Times Australia
body: Advanced Micro Devices Inc. shares jumped 9.5% on Wednesday. Strong results from AI cloud provider CoreWeave and an upbeat analyst report on server processors drove a broad rally in semiconductor stocks. AMD stock traded at $564.17 in afternoon trading, up 9.50%. It outpaced Nvidia, which gained about 5%. The move added to a sharp rebound from last week's AI selloff. The rally began after CoreWeave reported third-quarter results late Tuesday that beat analyst forecasts. The company reported revenue of $3.66 billion and raised its full-year 2026 revenue forecast to between $13.0 billion and $13.3 billion, according to The Motley Fool. CoreWeave also said it plans capital investment of $37 billion to $39 billion. Analysts said that points to continued heavy spending on data center chips, including AMD's processors. CoreWeave shares surged more than 25%. AMD also got a boost from a UBS report on server processor sales. UBS analyst Timothy Arcuri said server CPU shipments rose 31% from a year earlier in the third quarter. He said AMD's server CPU market share held steady at about 28.4%, while Intel's share fell 2.4 percentage points. Arcuri also believes CPU prices are rising, which could boost AMD's profit margins. He projected that CPU sales could reach $210 billion by 2030. At AMD's current market share, that would mean nearly $60 billion in CPU sales for the company. AI systems increasingly need powerful central processors alongside graphics chips, which has fueled demand for AMD's EPYC server processors. Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider said AI stocks were "clearly in oversold territory" and named AMD, Nvidia and Broadcom as top picks. He described AMD as "very attractive" for growth, though less compelling on valuation. AMD has a 12-month median price target of $650, based on 56 analysts, according to The Motley Fool. AMD shares have been extremely volatile. On Nov. 5, the S&P 500 fell 4.4% in its worst day of the year, while AMD dropped 17.3%, according to Trefis. The stock then rebounded more than 11% on Monday. CNBC's Jim Cramer called AMD a winner in a post on X, but warned that "a data center multi-year roadmap in this country is now suspect." AMD's year-to-date gain stood at about 140% as of Tuesday, according to Trefis. AMD reported record third-quarter revenue of $13.4 billion earlier this month, up 45% from a year earlier and above analyst expectations. Adjusted earnings per share came in at $2.09, up 74% and ahead of forecasts. Management said demand exceeds supply. The company increased inventory by about $3 billion in the quarter to $11.5 billion to meet strong data center demand. Free cash flow fell to $554 million in the quarter from $1.9 billion a year earlier, which management attributed to working capital and spending on capacity. AMD pairs its Instinct AI graphics chips with EPYC server processors in its Helios rack-scale systems. The company also runs PC, gaming and embedded chip businesses, giving it a broader revenue mix than Nvidia. This article is for informational purposes only and does not constitute investment advice.
